text: I’ll model the fluid as the union of the cylindrical chamber and four horizontal rectangular duct prisms. I interpret “40 mm above the floor” as the **lower edge** of each 30 mm-high port. Each duct inlet plane is 50 mm along its axis from the nominal cylinder-wall centreline intersection; the CAD prism continues slightly into the chamber solely to make a robust fluid union. The 15° angle is measured in plan from the local tangent toward the chamber, with all four ducts having the same swirl sense. I’ll use a coarse background mesh followed by body-fitted surface snapping after the geometry is verified.

The union is a single connected solid and the requested axis angles and nominal duct lengths measure correctly. I’ll now tessellate and inspect the coarse fluid envelope from an oblique view and from above, which is especially important here because the 15° near-tangential entry is not obvious from scalar bounds.

The preview exposed a placement error: `Cylinder` defaults to vertical centring, so its floor was at −0.1 m while the port elevations were measured from zero. I’ll correct the chamber to span z = 0…0.2 m and rebuild the union before doing any patch extraction.

With the corrected elevation, I’ll inspect the exact post-boolean boundary faces—their geometry types, centres, areas and normals—so patch membership is based on face provenance/orientation rather than a bounding-box guess. The top disk will then be deliberately split into the 40 mm outlet disk and surrounding top annulus.

The boolean boundary is cleanly interpretable: one cylindrical vessel-wall face, floor and top disks, and six planar faces per duct (four exposed wall pieces, one inlet, plus the top/bottom pieces). I’ll create the outlet disk and top annulus directly from concentric wires, then form named face compounds. Inlet faces are recognized by their original outer-plane centre and outward axis normal; each remaining duct face is assigned to the duct whose prism boundary contains it.
Before exporting, I’ll validate the exact face construction API and areas for the deliberately split top; this avoids discovering after meshing that the annulus and outlet overlap or leave a gap.

The split top areas sum exactly to the original chamber top area. I’ll now export the 12 requested patch files (`inlet1`…`inlet4`, `outlet`, `cylinderWall`, `floor`, `top`, and `ductWall1`…`ductWall4`) using a common tessellation tolerance so their shared edges coincide.

All requested patches are present with the expected counts and areas; each inlet is exactly \(20\times30\) mm. I’ll create a coarse 5 mm Cartesian background mesh around the envelope. SnappyHexMesh will retain the connected interior selected at the chamber centre and snap it to the 12 STL patches, with one refinement level at all surfaces (about 2.5 mm locally).

The background mesh is 54,432 uniform 5 mm cells and fully encloses the geometry. I’ll now run the coarse body-fitting pass and inspect its completion and patch creation before considering any refinement changes.

SnappyHexMesh stopped before modifying the mesh because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder discretisation dictionaries even for meshing. I’ll add minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` files, then rerun.
The required support dictionaries now exist. I’ll rerun the same coarse snapping pass.

The coarse body-fitted mesh completed with 52,136 cells, all surface cells at 2.5 or 5 mm refinement levels, and no snappy quality errors. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` assessment and inspect patch counts and topology.

The exhaustive geometry mode reports 1,452 cells as concave under face-plane decomposition, although all standard quality metrics are good (max non-orthogonality 52.6°, max skewness 0.568, positive volumes and determinants). Because completion uses the standard binding check, I’ll run the standard `checkMesh` explicitly; if it also fails, I’ll revise the meshing method rather than waive it.

The binding standard check passes: one connected region, all 12 patches, positive cell volumes, max non-orthogonality 52.6°, max skewness 0.568, and `Mesh OK`. I’ll visually inspect the final boundary mesh, including a top view where all four angled ducts and the outlet/top split are visible.
The converter confirms that every requested boundary exists as a distinct mesh patch. I’ll render those patch meshes with distinct colours and visible mesh edges.

Final mesh summary:

- Built the gas volume of a **0.120 m ID × 0.200 m** cylindrical chamber.
- Four ports measure **0.020 × 0.030 m**, with lower edges at **z = 0.040 m**.
- Each inlet centreline measures **0.050000 m** from its inlet plane to the nominal vessel-wall intersection and **15.000000°** from the local tangent; all use the same swirl sense.
- The outlet is a **0.040 m diameter** disk at the centre of the top.
- Exported all 12 requested STL patches to `constant/triSurface`.
- Final mesh: **52,136 cells**, one connected region, 12 boundary patches; standard `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**. Max non-orthogonality is **52.61°**, max skewness **0.568**.
- Assumptions: “40 mm above the floor” means the port lower edge; no outlet duct was added because no outlet length was specified; the coarse mesh uses 5 mm background cells and approximately 2.5 mm surface cells. CAD duct prisms extend 35 mm internally only to ensure a robust union; this extension does not alter the final chamber envelope.
- Additional exhaustive `checkMesh -allGeometry -allTopology` flagged 1,452 concave snapped cells, while all standard/binding checks, volumes, determinants, face pyramids, interpolation weights, and volume ratios passed. No solver suitability beyond mesh geometry/quality was assessed.

The advisory surface checks found that independently tessellating each patch re-sampled shared CAD edges differently; the CAD solid and OpenFOAM mesh are closed, but the union of the separately generated STL triangles is not watertight and contains crossing pairs. I’ll fix the exports by tessellating the complete named face assembly once with OpenCASCADE, then writing each patch from that shared triangulation so adjacent STL files use identical edge nodes.
The shared meshing call succeeded; only my null-handle probe used an outdated OpenCASCADE method. I’ll inspect the installed triangulation interface and then use its actual node/triangle accessors.
I’ll re-emit the shared tessellation setup in a self-contained cell so it is reproducible in `build.py`.

The shared CAD assembly now has one persistent triangulation. I’ll overwrite each patch STL using triangles from that assembly, preserving face orientation and transformations while keeping each requested patch in its own file.

The shared export greatly reduces the triangle count while preserving the exact CAD tolerance. Before remeshing, I’ll test the welded union of all 12 new STL files for closure and self-intersection using OpenFOAM’s surface checker.

The first shared attempt still assembled already-detached faces, so OpenCASCADE did not preserve the solid’s common top/floor/cylinder edges. I’ll instead imprint the outlet circle directly into the top face of the **solid**, producing a topologically split but volumetrically unchanged solid, and tessellate that complete solid. First I’ll inspect the installed face-splitting API.
The installed kernel provides `BRepFeat_SplitShape.Add`, which can add a wire to a basis face. I’ll inspect its overloads and then apply the circular wire to the original top disk.
I’ll now split the solid’s original top face with the exact 20 mm-radius wire and verify that the operation preserves one solid and the original volume while creating two coplanar top faces.
The split itself completed, but the generic build123d cast helper does not wrap this returned topological type. I’ll wrap the resulting OpenCASCADE solid explicitly and repeat the invariants.

The solid is now topologically correct: one solid, 28 faces, unchanged volume to machine precision, with top areas exactly matching the outlet disk and annulus. I’ll rebuild the named groups from this split solid, then clean and tessellate the entire solid in one pass so every patch boundary is a genuinely shared topological edge.
The final groups again contain exactly the intended faces. I’ll overwrite the 12 STLs from the solid-wide triangulation and immediately check their welded union.

The welded STL union now passes: **closed**, one connected part, one consistent normal zone, and no illegal triangles. I’ll rebuild the Cartesian background mesh so the final OpenFOAM mesh is regenerated from these corrected STL files.
The clean background mesh is restored. I’ll run the final body-fitting pass against the watertight, conformal patch STLs.
The corrected STL set produces the same intended 52,136-cell mesh and snappy reports no quality errors. I’ll run the final standard check once more on this regenerated mesh.
